Femmes sans statut : entre précarité, si: Women Without Status: Between Precarity, Silence and Dignity
À Montréal, des femmes sans statut trava: In Montréal, women without status work in the shadows, without protections or care. A report on precarity, dignity and invisibility.
En décembre 2023, l’ancien ministre fédé: In December 2023, former federal Immigration Minister Marc Miller estimated that there could be up to 600,000 undocumented people in Canada. Photo credit: María Gabriela Aguzzi
Depuis que j’ai commencé à faire du jour: Since I started working as a journalist in Montréal more than 13 years ago, the Centre des travailleuses et travailleurs immigrants (CTTI) has helped me better understand the realities of Latin American migrants in the city.
C’est aussi grâce à cet organisme que j’: It was also through this organization that I met Nina González, a woman of Colombian origin whose profile we published in La Converse to highlight her activism for women’s rights, even though she lives without immigration status.
Le 3 décembre, le CTTI donnait une confé: On December 3, the CTTI held a press conference to present the results of several years of research based on surveys of women without status, in an attempt to document their working conditions and their access to health care.
J’ai assisté à l’événement et discuté av: I attended the event and spoke with Viviana Medina, a worker and community organizer with the CTTI. Once the mainstream media cameras had switched off, she introduced me to Cindy and Sara, two Mexican women of different ages and backgrounds, but bound by the same reality: lives marked by unstable, poorly paid piecework, and by the constant uncertainty of wondering whether staying in Montréal without papers is really the best option. They say they cannot go back to their hometowns, where the violence they fled awaits them.
Elles donnent un visage et une voix aux: They give a face and a voice to the statistics presented in the study.
Voici leurs histoires et les principaux: Here are their stories and the main findings of the CTTI’s research.
Elles sont des milliers à Montréal, cons: There are thousands of them in Montréal, an essential yet hidden part of the city. For these women of flesh, bone and dignity, the lack of papers is not just an administrative issue; it is a true “psychological cage” and an existence marked by daily uncertainty and forced invisibility.
Vivant dans l’ombre d’un marché du trava: Living in the shadow of a labour market that often operates with complete impunity, these women hold precarious jobs, notably in cleaning or care work, for an average income of only $319 a week. Whether they were “guardian angels” during the pandemic or fled violence in their countries of origin, they face abusive working conditions and virtually no access to health care without a RAMQ card. For many, the constant fear of deportation or of an unpayable hospital bill ends up becoming a “second skin.”
C’est pour dénoncer cette réalité que pl: It was to denounce this reality that several of them spoke out in early December 2025, at a press conference organized by the Centre des travailleuses et travailleurs immigrants (CTTI) to mark the launch of the report Femmes sans statut en action : conditions de travail et santé.
Après les caméras et les discours, la te: After the cameras and the speeches, the tension eased in the kitchen of the Y des femmes de Montréal. Far from the microphones and official presentations, the atmosphere softened, letting more fragile, more intimate voices emerge, those of women like Cindy* and Sara*.
Autour d’elles, les bénévoles du Comité: Around them, volunteers from the Women’s Committee share a meal. The murmur of their conversations, still heavy with what was just said publicly, creates a temporary refuge.
C’est dans cet espace improvisé que Cind: In this improvised space, Cindy*, 39, finally takes off the mask she had worn since the start of the event. Her face appears: cheerful, radiant, almost at odds with the harshness of her story. Small Christmas earrings sparkle at her ears.
À quelques pas, Sara* met la main aux de:
A few steps away, Sara* helps with the last preparations for the lunch the migrant support organization is offering to participants. She does not take off her mask, which hides her face. Her eyes are like open windows onto her sadness, and deep dark circles bear witness to the insomnia she has endured “for years.”

Cindy and Sara are the human face, often unseen, of the statistics revealed by the CTTI after five years of research.
Cindy a l’énergie de celles qui cherchen: Cindy has the energy of someone who is still looking for “the positive side of life,” as she puts it. Sara embodies the exhaustion of a decade spent in the shadows, as she describes her situation. Together, they tell the story of everyday life in a city, Montréal, that also runs on their work, but too often refuses to recognize their contribution.

Photo credit: María Gabriela Aguzzi
Malgré leurs histoires individuelles, el: Despite their individual stories, they are part of a much larger reality that is hard to measure: no one knows for certain how many women without status live in Montréal, or in Canada. According to figures cited by the federal government, the total number of undocumented people in the country could reach half a million. In December 2023, former federal Immigration Minister Marc Miller even suggested that the figure could climb as high as 600,000. Either way, this population remains very difficult to count because of the precariousness of its status.
Pour comprendre le sourire défiant de Ci: To understand Cindy’s defiant smile, you have to know her story. She arrived in Canada in 2017 with her husband, after he was the victim of a violent robbery in Mexico City.
Lorsque tout a fermé durant la pandémie,: When everything shut down during the pandemic, Cindy went out to work. “I’ve always liked helping people,” she says. That is why, in the midst of the health crisis, she decided to study and work as an orderly in a private seniors’ residence.
Cindy a tenu la main des aînés québécois: Cindy held the hands of Quebec seniors in their final moments, strictly following protocols to protect the most vulnerable.
« À ce moment, ils avaient besoin d’aide: “At that time, they needed help,” she recalls. While she was caring for citizens, she was convinced that her immigration file was moving forward, with the help of her lawyer. But in 2023, she learned that she should have left the country two years earlier.
Elle explique que, en raison de la pandé: She explains that, because of the pandemic, they had not received the information about their deportation on time, and that the reason they were given for the delay was precisely that the pandemic had delayed everything.
Les autorités de l’Immigration les ont c: Immigration authorities contacted them directly, and that was when they were told they had to leave the country within a maximum of 20 days, because their refugee claim had been rejected.
« Pour moi, c’était très injuste », dit-:
“To me, it was very unfair,” she says. From 2017 to 2023, Cindy and her husband built a life: cars, taxes paid, plans to buy a house. Suddenly, they were given 20 days to settle their affairs and leave the country.

They did not leave. “We decided to stay like that, because it was really too complicated to do everything in 20 days,” Cindy explains. Going back to Mexico was not an option: violence was waiting for them there. And so, “the ‘guardian angel’ of the pandemic became a woman without status.”

Today, Cindy’s smile is her shield, but her reality remains precarious: she lives off “calls people pass on to me for work,” cleaning homes or helping at events for about $20 an hour, without knowing whether she will have work the next day. “A daily uncertainty,” she says.
Les yeux de Sara se remplissent de larme:
Sara’s eyes fill with tears. Her story is a reminder of how fragile a migrant’s fate can be. She arrived in Montréal 10 years ago, also from Mexico and also fleeing violence.

Her son, a truck driver, was the unwitting witness of an execution. After that event, he was persecuted, which pushed the family to leave the country almost immediately.
À son arrivée au Canada, Sara a cherché: When she arrived in Canada, Sara looked for help but found none. “I had a lawyer, but I didn’t get enough help,” she laments.
Après avoir reçu une réponse négative à: After receiving a negative response to her refugee claim, she filed a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) application as a last resort to show that she could not return to Mexico. It was then that her lawyer gave her a piece of advice that would seal her fate: he told her to submit “some kind of story,” beyond her own flight from violence, believing it would strengthen her file.
« Cela m’a déconcertée, mais c’était mon: “It threw me off, but he was my lawyer. I trusted him,” she says.
Sa demande d’ERAR a été refusée et, depu: Her PRRA application was rejected and, since then, she has lived with what she describes as “an emotional instability that affects everything.” The lack of papers is not only an administrative problem, it is also a psychological cage.
« C’est une obscurité qu’on vit », dit-e: “It’s a darkness we live in,” she says in a broken voice. “We have neither peace nor quiet… We live in waiting… It’s truly desperate,” Sara confides.
<strong>Une radiographie des conditions: An X-ray of the conditions of women without status
Ce que Cindy et Sara vivent, le rapport:
What Cindy and Sara are living through, the CTTI report confirms with numbers. The study, conducted with 72 women without status, sheds light on a hidden labour market operating with complete impunity.

According to the report, these women’s average income is $319 a week, for an average of 30 hours of work per week, plus about 2 hours of commuting per day.
Qui plus est, 25 % des répondantes n’ont:
What’s more, 25% of respondents have never received the legal minimum wage in Quebec, which is $16.10 an hour.

Domestic work and cleaning, the sectors where Sara and Cindy work, are fertile ground for abuse. Sara explains it precisely: “They tell you: ‘I’ll pay you three or four hours, but the house has two or three bathrooms, two floors, a kitchen… You have to work fast if you want to earn those four hours.’”
C’est une course contre la montre et con: It is a race against the clock and against one’s own body. No breaks, no paid overtime and, according to respondents, wage theft is more common than one might think.
De plus, chez ces femmes, la peur du lic:
Moreover, among these women, the fear of being fired is mixed with stifling surveillance: 41% of them feel excessively monitored by their employers or recruiters.

It is an environment where stress is a condition of work: 66% of workers report stress levels above 8 out of 10 because of their working conditions.
L’étude du CTTI est dédiée à la mémoire:
The CTTI study is dedicated to the memory of Yolanda and Lulu, two women who died prematurely. The committee says their deaths illustrate the reality of women without status. In February 2020, Yolanda González died of breast cancer at 32. Without a RAMQ card and without access to preventive care, she was taken by the disease.

Seven months later, Lourdes Castro, known as Lulu, also lost her life. A domestic worker, she had suffered two workplace accidents – two falls – in her final year and had developed an intestinal illness that was never diagnosed.

The CTTI’s Women’s Committee says Yolanda and Lulu died because they had no immigration status and were exposed to extremely difficult working conditions, which deteriorated their health.
Pour Cindy, Sara et bien d’autres femmes:
For Cindy, Sara and many other women without status, health remains an unattainable luxury: 49% of the illnesses reported by participants are directly related to work.

Cindy has asthma, a manageable but costly condition. In Quebec, she cannot legally buy an inhaler without a prescription and has no doctor to get one. Her survival depends on the black market.
« Une personne mexicaine me les procure: “A Mexican person gets them for me; she sells me her son’s inhalers, he’s also asthmatic,” Cindy says. Each inhaler costs $130, and she needs two.
Sara souffre de saignements rectaux depu:
Sara has suffered from rectal bleeding for more than a year. The fear of the hospital bill paralyzes her, but when the pain becomes unbearable, she goes to the emergency room.

She is treated, but the bill comes to $2,000 for a few hours of care and tests, with no hospital stay. For a woman who earns as little as she does, it is a considerable sum.
Cependant, elle fait preuve d’une dignit: Yet she shows unshakeable dignity: “Whether I’m alive or dead, I don’t like owing money to anyone, that’s my peace,” she says firmly.
Elle rembourse peu à peu sa dette à l’hô: She is paying off her debt to the hospital bit by bit: $180 one month, $600 the next. “It’s not in my principles to leave without paying,” she insists, even if it sometimes forces her to sacrifice her own subsistence.
Tant Cindy que Sara ont eu recours à plu: Both Cindy and Sara have turned to Médecins du Monde several times. It is an international humanitarian organization that provides medical care to vulnerable people, including people without papers. Its mission focuses on offering essential health services, support and guidance to those who face barriers to accessing the public health system, but its resources are limited and, as a result, it cannot always help everyone who needs it.
<strong>Le poids invisible : santé menta: The invisible weight: mental health and family
Le rapport sur la santé mentale de la mê:
The mental health report from the same study indicates that depression and anxiety are pervasive among respondents.

Sara lives with a heavy heart, not only for herself but also for her son. At 40, he lives in deep depression, terrified of going outside. “It’s exhausting to see him like this; he lives in constant fear,” Sara confides.
Le traumatisme de la persécution au Mexi:
The trauma of persecution in Mexico mixes with the trauma of living in hiding in Canada, leaving him paralyzed.

Many women also carry the weight of two families: the one living here and the one left behind. As many as 65% of them send money to their country of origin, an average of $640 a month, often at the expense of their own basic needs.

Fear has become a “second skin,” says Nina González, also a member of the Women’s Committee, echoing several testimonies. They are afraid to report sexual abuse, to demand a wage, to grow old without a pension.
Malgré ce tableau sombre, le comité y vo: Despite this bleak picture, the committee sees an act of resistance in it. The simple fact of presenting this study – the full version of which will be published in 2026 – is a political act that, according to Nina González, gives them back their dignity.
Le comité exige l’accès à la RAMQ, l’acc: The committee demands access to the RAMQ, access to emergency services for physical and mental health, open work permits, access to the Régie des rentes du Québec, access to the federal pension plan, access to employment insurance, and the creation of a regularization program for people without status.
Alors que les participantes, issues de d:
As participants from different backgrounds take off their masks to eat, Cindy and Sara share their thoughts.

Cindy asks for pragmatism and recognition: “We need a glimmer of hope. We suffer in silence,” she says. She highlights the contribution of her fellow members: they speak English and French, have degrees and work hard. “Let’s hope that one day the government will look at us, because we are suffering,” she says.

Sara souhaite aller au-delà des considér: Sara wants to go beyond economic considerations. If she had the Immigration Minister in front of her, she would not talk to him about laws, but about humanity.
« Je lui demanderais, par humanité, d’av:
“I would ask him, out of humanity, to have compassion for everyone in our situation… that this life is really fleeting,” says Sara. And her plea is also for young people, for her son, so that they are not consumed by this “darkness.”

“They [the politicians] have children too… That’s what I would ask them… We are human, may they have pity on us,” Sara concludes.
En sortant du bâtiment, Cindy, Sara et t:
As they leave the building, Cindy, Sara and all those who wore a T-shirt that day with the slogan “Femmes sans statut en action” melt into the crowd. They become invisible again. For many of the people around them, their acquaintances, they may be just people who clean an office or care for an elderly person.

But the report left on the table explains who they are: an essential yet hidden part of the city, women of flesh, bone and dignity who, despite a system that renders them invisible, persist in existing.

À Montréal, des milliers de femmes sans: In Montréal, thousands of women without status live in precarity, invisibility and fear. This report, backed by a CTTI study, reveals their abusive working conditions, their restricted access to health care and the human consequences of a failing immigration system.
